title: New ACCC merger rules unfairly cover family businesses, car dealers say
full_text:
Car dealers say they are the unintended victims of new merger oversight rules designed to ensure large acquisitions cannot proceed without tougher regulatory scrutiny, warning that the regime unfairly captures small and medium family-owned businesses that pose no competition risks.
From January 1, businesses have been required to notify the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission of proposed acquisitions that meet specific turnover thresholds and secure its approval before a deal can proceed.
Simply filing an acquisition notification costs $56,800, while requesting an exemption costs $8300. For more complex reviews, the ACCC can charge fees of up to $1.6 million.
The ACCC must be notified if the buyer and the seller have a combined turnover of at least $200 million, provided they generate $50 million locally or the global transaction value exceeds $250 million. A proposed transaction must also be reported if a buyer making $500 million or more acquires an Australian target earning more than $10 million.
The Australian Automotive Dealers Association, citing research commissioned by it and authored by consulting and advisory firm BDO, said the new rules would unfairly capture car dealerships, which generate high turnover but operate on thin margins because of the high costs of inventories. BDO estimates between 20 and 30 dealership transactions occur each year, with most expected to be caught by the scheme.
"This report confirms what AADA has been saying since the merger reforms were announced, that franchised new car dealerships are not the types of businesses these laws were designed to target," said AADA chief executive James Voortman.
The rules were put in place in response to growing community pressure for the federal government to counter the dominance of Coles and Woolworths in the supermarket sector.
Coles' purchase of land for a new supermarket in Kalgoorlie last month was the first acquisition blocked under the scheme. The company has since disputed the ruling.
Sellers must also lodge transactions on the regulator's public register, prompting fears that staff could resign after learning of sales or competitors may attempt to disrupt them.
BDO's research said that unlike the supermarket sector, the Australian dealership market was competitive, with more than 67 car brands sold across 3910 franchised dealerships.
ASX-listed Eagers Automotive holds a 14 per cent market share, and the next-largest, Peter Warren Group and Autosports Group, each holds 2 per cent.
"Unlike other industries, dealership competition is already heavily shaped by manufacturers through franchise agreements, dealer network planning and ownership limits," said Voortman.
According to BDO, a high-performing car dealership with a $100 million turnover generated a margin of only 3.5 per cent, with margins already under threat as the proliferation of Chinese electric vehicles puts downward pressure on profit per vehicle.
Todd Blewitt sold his second-generation car dealership in Coffs Harbour last October, two months before the new merger rules started. He said his dealership had an annual turnover of $100 million but operated at a margin of 2 per cent. "It very much feels to me like a tax."
The ACCC and Treasury did not respond to requests for comment.
